claims.text: The starting alloy has a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar colony microstructure.
Relatively coherent lamellar interfaces promote dislocation pile-ups.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries generate local stress concentrations, microcracking, and brittle room-temperature failure.
A post-solidification annealing treatment can selectively increase lamellar-boundary incoherency.
The proposed annealing can modify the boundaries without changing the alloy's overall phase composition.
Less-coherent interlamellar boundaries absorb or disperse dislocations more effectively than the original coherent boundaries.
Annealing induces controlled atomic-scale disorder at the lamellar boundaries.
Boundary disorder mitigates dislocation pile-up formation.
Mitigating dislocation pile-ups reduces local stress concentrations and microcrack nucleation.
The annealing treatment retains the dual-phase lamellar morphology.
Retaining the dual-phase lamellar morphology preserves the strength supplied by the eutectic structure.
The annealed alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the untreated alloy.
The annealed alloy will maintain or slightly increase tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The predicted improvement applies to room-temperature tensile testing at standard strain rates.
Over-annealing may excessively relax the boundaries and reduce strength.
Under-annealing will not sufficiently reduce dislocation pile-ups.

contradictions.description: The intervention proposes controlled boundary 'decohesion' as interchangeable with increased incoherency, whereas the mechanism requires intact but dislocation-absorbing interfaces and the outcome requires preserved strength. Decohesion denotes loss of interfacial bonding and could instead facilitate interfacial cracking; it is not equivalent to reduced coherency.
